transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

I came in because my head just feels foggy lately. I keep mixing up simple things—appointment times, dates for exhibits, and even which volunteer I already called. It’s not like me, and it’s been bothering me.
Have you noticed any difficulty remembering recent events or learning new information?

Yes, I have. It’s mostly recent things—I’ll get appointment times mixed up, or confuse the dates for exhibits. Sometimes I can’t remember whether I already called a volunteer or not. It just feels like my head is foggy, and that’s not normal for me.
Have you had trouble remembering things from the past, like important events or information you used to know well?
No, I don’t think so. Things from years ago—important events, people I’ve known, that kind of thing—seem okay to me. It’s more the recent stuff that gets mixed up.
Do you ever feel confused about where you are, what day it is, or why you’re doing something?

I don’t think so. I mean, I know where I am and why I’m there. I might lose track of the date now and then if I haven’t looked at the calendar, but I don’t feel confused like I don’t know what’s going on.
Have you ever felt disoriented or confused in certain situations, such as not knowing where you were or who you were with, even briefly?
No, I can’t say that’s happened. I don’t recall ever not knowing where I was or who I was with. It’s more that I might be a little forgetful, but not disoriented like that.
Have you had trouble planning or organizing things, like managing your schedule or handling tasks that you used to do easily?

Yes, I have. That’s really part of what brought me in. My head feels foggy, and I keep mixing up simple things—appointment times, dates for exhibits, even which volunteer I already called. Things I used to keep straight are just harder to organize now.
Have you had trouble handling more complex tasks, like following a new recipe, managing finances, or figuring out how to use a new gadget?

Yes, I think so. Mostly my head just feels foggy, and I mix up things I used to keep straight—like appointment times, dates for exhibits, or whether I already called a certain volunteer. It makes anything with several steps feel harder than it should.
Have you had trouble making decisions or thinking through problems clearly, more so than before?

Yes, more than before. I feel like my head is foggy, and I don’t think things through as clearly. I keep mixing up simple things—appointments, exhibit dates, or whether I already called someone—and then it’s harder to decide what to do next.
Have you noticed yourself making decisions that you later realized were poor or out of character for you, such as in personal matters or at work?

Yes… not so much big reckless decisions, but I do find I’m making mistakes that don’t feel like me. My head feels foggy, and I mix up simple things—appointment times, exhibit dates, or which volunteer I already called—and then I realize later I didn’t handle it right.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to manage your usual responsibilities at work or home, or in your interactions with others, that weren't a problem before?

Yes. I’ve missed doctor visits, and I’ve gotten the senior center schedule so mixed up that it caused problems. My husband has had to step in more—helping me with phone calls, keeping the calendar straight, and even making repair decisions that I used to handle on my own. It’s frustrating, because those were normal things for me before.
Have you had any trouble recognizing familiar objects, faces, or places, even though your vision seems fine? For example, not recognizing a common object or a family member just by looking at them?
No, I don’t think so. I recognize my family and familiar places. I haven’t had trouble looking at an object or a person and not knowing what it is.

Have you noticed any changes in your ability to judge situations or make decisions appropriately, such as difficulty assessing risks or understanding consequences, beyond just forgetting things or feeling confused?

I’m not sure I’d say that. I haven’t really noticed myself misunderstanding risks or consequences in a big way. It feels more like I get mixed up or forget details, and then the decision comes out wrong because of that.
Have you noticed yourself pulling back from social activities or interactions, like avoiding events or spending less time with friends or family, more than before?

Yes, I think so. I don’t do much of what I used to enjoy. My watercolors just sit there, and I haven’t been tending my tomato plants like I used to. I used to like line dancing and watching the cardinals out back, but now I just can’t seem to make myself care about any of it.
Have you been aware that you were making mistakes or having memory problems before others pointed them out to you?

Yes, I was noticing it myself. That’s really what brought me in—my head has felt foggy, and I keep mixing up simple things, like appointment times, exhibit dates, or which volunteer I already called. Others may notice too, but I knew something wasn’t right.
Have you had any trouble finding your way around familiar places, like getting lost in your own neighborhood or having difficulty with directions?
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t gotten lost in my neighborhood or anything like that. Directions haven’t really been the main problem, at least not that I’ve noticed.

Can you describe how different these memory and thinking problems are compared to how you were before—have they significantly changed how you function day-to-day, or is it more of a mild inconvenience that comes and goes?

It’s more than a mild inconvenience now. I’ve missed doctor visits, and I’ve gotten the senior center schedule so mixed up that it caused real problems. My husband has had to step in with calls and calendars, and even decisions about repairs—things I used to handle myself without much trouble.
Would you say your memory and thinking problems have caused a noticeable decline in your ability to function in your everyday life compared to how you were before?

Yes, I would. It’s been a real decline for me. I’ve missed doctor visits, and I’ve gotten the senior center schedule so mixed up that my husband has had to step in with the calls and calendars. He’s also helping with repair decisions now—things I used to handle on my own.
Would you say your memory and thinking problems have caused a noticeable decline in your ability to function in your everyday life compared to how you were before?

Yes. Like I said, it’s definitely noticeable. I’ve missed doctor visits, and I got the senior center schedule all mixed up. My husband’s had to take over helping with phone calls and calendars, and even decisions about repairs—things I used to manage myself.
